passage:
"Switch off now, Ujjwal."
"Papa, I'm at the key part!"
"It's been an hour."
"Five more minutes! You always ruin everything!"
Kishore folded his arms and waited. Ujjwal's face burned. He heard his own voice and winced.
"Sorry, Papa. I hate being stopped in the middle."
"I know. Tomorrow, tell me before you start, and we'll agree you finish the round."
The next evening: "One round, Papa."
"One round."
When it ended, Ujjwal switched off by himself. Kishore ruffled his hair.

qa.q: How long had Ujjwal been playing when his father asked him to stop?
Why did Ujjwal shout at his father?
qa.a: He felt angry at being interrupted at the key part of the game, and his burning face shows the anger was strong.

qa.q: What agreement keeps the peace between Ujjwal and his father?
qa.a: Agreeing before he starts that he will finish the round and then stop, as they did the next evening 🙂.

qa.q: How might Kishore have felt when Ujjwal shouted?
qa.a: Probably frustrated at being shouted at, but he stayed calm and offered a plan, which suggests he cared more about a solution than about winning the moment.

grounding: Illustrates a child shouting at a parent who says switch off, and the calm agreement to finish the round then stop.

passage: Deepika, come, stop scowling. You shouted at your Ammi about the game? Let me tell you what your Khala did at your age. Our family had one old computer, and I was mad about an online racing game. One evening my Ammi, your Nani, called, "Parveen, switch it off, now!" I was on the last lap. I screamed, "I'm at the most important part!" She walked over and pulled the plug. I lost the whole race and shouted so loudly the neighbours heard. The next day, when we had both cooled down, Ammi said, "Tell me before you start how long a race is." So we agreed: I would say "one race" first, finish it, and get up. Most days it worked, and the shouting stopped.

qa.q: What did Nani do when young Parveen screamed about the last lap?
qa.a: She walked over and pulled the plug.

qa.q: Why did young Parveen scream at Ammi?
qa.a: Parveen felt angry and frustrated at being interrupted on the last lap.

qa.q: Which choice in Khala's story ended the fights, and why?
qa.a: Agreeing before starting to play one race and then get up; nobody was cut off mid-race, so there was less to shout about.

qa.q: How might Parveen's Ammi have seen the moment she pulled the plug?
qa.a: She probably felt ignored and fed up after calling, and wanted to be listened to.

grounding: An aunt recalls shouting at her mother for interrupting a game and how agreeing on "one race" beforehand kept the peace.

passage:
The auto was already honking outside when Seema called, "Akash, phone off, we're leaving for the wedding!"
"Mumma, I'm at the boss level! Two minutes!" Akash shouted without looking up.
"The driver is waiting. Now!"
"You ALWAYS do this!" He threw a cushion. Seema's jaw tightened, and she took the phone and switched it off. Akash sulked through the whole ride, arms folded, his new kurta scratching his neck.
At the wedding he watched his cousins laughing and felt silly. On the drive back he mumbled, "Sorry for shouting. Next time can you tell me earlier? Then I'll finish the round and stop."
Seema squeezed his hand. "Deal. A warning at ten minutes, then off."

qa.q: Where was the family going when Seema called Akash?
How did Akash feel watching his cousins laugh at the wedding?
qa.a: He felt silly and a bit ashamed of his shouting and sulking.

qa.q: What plan did Akash and Seema agree on?
qa.a: A warning at ten minutes, so Akash can finish the round and then stop.

qa.q: How did Seema see the moment Akash threw the cushion?
qa.a: Seema, rushed by the honking auto, felt tense and fed up, so she took the phone.

grounding: A boy shouts at his mother for interrupting a game, then agrees on an early warning so he can finish the round and stop.
